_comment: Per-work orientation descriptions shown in Browse Corpus and the Reader. Keyed by language, then by base work id (the .tess filename without language directory, extension, or .part suffix). Two or three plain sentences: what the work is, who wrote it and when, and why a reader might care. Every text import should add its entry here.

la.justin.epitome: Justin, probably writing in the second or third century AD, condensed the lost forty-four book universal history of Pompeius Trogus into this epitome. It is our main narrative source for much of Macedonian and Hellenistic history, and it was among the most widely read history books of the Middle Ages.
la.hyginus.fabulae: A handbook of roughly three hundred short mythological summaries compiled under the name of Hyginus, perhaps in the second century AD. The Latin is plain and sometimes garbled, but the collection preserves the plots of many Greek myths and lost tragedies found nowhere else.
la.hyginus.astronomica: A handbook of star lore attributed to the same Hyginus as the Fabulae. It tells the myths behind the constellations, explaining who each figure was and how they were placed in the sky, drawing on the Greek catasterism tradition.
la.isidore.etymologiae: Isidore, bishop of Seville (about 560 to 636), organized all the learning available to him into this twenty-book encyclopedia, approaching each subject through the origins of its words. It became the most influential reference work of the Middle Ages and preserves fragments of many ancient authors now lost.
la.petrarch.africa: Petrarch's Latin epic in nine books on Scipio Africanus and the Second Punic War, begun in 1338 and never finished to his satisfaction. He expected it to secure his fame, and its promise helped win him the poet laureate's crown in Rome in 1341.
la.pomponius_mela.de_chorographia: The earliest surviving geography in Latin, written around AD 43. In three brisk books Mela tours the coasts of the known world from the Strait of Gibraltar around Africa, Asia, and Europe, mixing description with marvels.
la.varro.de_lingua_latina: Varro (116 to 27 BC), the greatest scholar of republican Rome, wrote twenty-five books on the Latin language, of which books five through ten survive. They treat etymology and word formation and are a major source for archaic Latin and Roman antiquarian lore.
la.varro.res_rusticae: A dialogue on farming in three books, written by Varro in 37 BC when he was eighty. It covers the estate, livestock, and the profitable luxury trades of villa life such as aviaries and fishponds, and with Cato's treatise it is our chief Roman work on agriculture.
la.velleius_paterculus.historiae_romanae: A compendium of Roman history from the origins to AD 30, in two books, by a career officer who served under Tiberius. It is known for its admiring portrait of Tiberius and for capsule sketches of Latin literary history found nowhere else.
la.frontinus.strategemata: Frontinus (about AD 40 to 103), a senator and general, collected historical stratagems arranged by type as a casebook for commanders. Each chapter offers short examples of how past generals handled a recurring problem of war.
la.frontinus.de_aquis: An administrative treatise on the aqueducts of Rome, written when Frontinus was appointed their curator in AD 97. It gives a unique inside view of a great Roman public work: the history of each aqueduct, its measurements, and the frauds he uncovered.
la.sidonius.carmina: The poems of Sidonius Apollinaris (about 430 to 486), a Gallo-Roman aristocrat who became bishop of Clermont. They include verse panegyrics of three emperors and occasional pieces for friends, written in an elaborate late antique style.
la.sidonius.epistulae: Nine books of literary letters modeled on Pliny, from the last generation of Roman aristocratic life in Gaul. Sidonius describes villas, dinner parties, book collections, and church politics while Roman rule in the West dissolved around him.
la.fronto.epistulae: The correspondence of Marcus Cornelius Fronto (about 95 to 166), the leading orator of his day and tutor to Marcus Aurelius, recovered from a palimpsest in 1815. The letters exchange affection, advice on rhetoric, and news of health and family with the future emperor.
la.nemesianus.eclogae: Four pastoral poems by Nemesianus of Carthage, written in the later third century AD. They carry the bucolic tradition of Virgil and Calpurnius Siculus into late antiquity, with shepherds singing of love, loss, and song itself.
la.nemesianus.cynegetica: A didactic poem on hunting by Nemesianus, written about AD 283. It treats the breeding and training of dogs and horses and the huntsman's gear before breaking off after 325 lines.
la.nemesianus_pseudo.de_aucupio: Two short fragments on bird catching transmitted under the name of Nemesianus. Their authorship is doubted, but they preserve a small sample of ancient fowling lore in verse.
la.symmachus.epistulae: The collected letters of Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (about 345 to 402), the leading pagan senator of his generation, published in ten books on the model of Pliny. They are the classic picture of late Roman senatorial networking, and Symmachus is best remembered for his plea to restore the Altar of Victory to the senate house.
la.abelard.historia_calamitatum: Peter Abelard (1079 to 1142) tells the story of his own misfortunes in this long autobiographical letter: his rise as the most famous philosopher and teacher in Paris, his love affair with Heloise, his castration, and his troubles as a monk.
la.abelard.epistolae: The correspondence between Abelard and Heloise that followed the Historia calamitatum, together with letters of spiritual direction for Heloise's convent. It is among the most famous exchanges of letters of the Middle Ages, moving between passionate memory and monastic counsel.
la.gregorius_magnus.dialogi: Four books of miracle stories about the holy men of Italy, written by Pope Gregory the Great around 593. The second book is a life of St. Benedict and is the principal source for his biography.
la.gregorius_magnus.regula_pastoralis: Gregory the Great's handbook on the office of bishop, written soon after he became pope in 590. It describes who should undertake pastoral rule and how to adapt teaching to different kinds of people, and it shaped the medieval ideal of church leadership. King Alfred had it translated into Old English.
la.lactantius_placidus.in_statii_thebaida_c: The ancient line-by-line commentary on Statius's Thebaid that goes under the name of Lactantius Placidus, compiled perhaps in the fifth or sixth century AD. Its notes explain mythology, geography, and diction, and they preserve a great deal of mythographic learning that would otherwise be lost.
la.aquinas.summa_theologiae_1: The First Part (Prima Pars) of Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae (c. 1265-1268), the most influential work of medieval scholastic theology: 119 questions on God, creation, angels, and human nature, each argued through objections, a magisterial answer, and replies. Aquinas quotes constantly - Scripture, Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Dionysius - which makes the Summa a crossroads for tracing how classical and patristic texts were read in the thirteenth century. Its question-and-article structure (cited as Ia q. 2 a. 3) became the standard form of university argument.
la.aquinas.hymni: The five eucharistic hymns attributed to Thomas Aquinas for the feast of Corpus Christi (1264): Pange lingua gloriosi, Lauda Sion, Sacris solemniis, Verbum supernum prodiens, and Adoro te devote. Sung continuously for seven centuries (Tantum ergo and O salutaris hostia are stanzas of the first two), they are among the most-quoted Latin verses ever written, and their opening lines deliberately echo earlier hymns by Venantius Fortunatus - intertextuality in liturgical action.
la.erasmus.moriae_encomium: Erasmus's Praise of Folly (1511), the most famous satire of the Renaissance, written in a week at Thomas More's house and punning on his name (Moriae encomium = 'praise of More'). Folly herself delivers a mock oration celebrating her indispensability to every human pursuit, skewering scholars, courtiers, monks, and theologians. The Latin is saturated with classical allusion - Lucian, Horace, and the proverbs Erasmus collected in his Adagia - making it a showcase of how antiquity was redeployed for satire.
la.erasmus.colloquia: A selection of eighteen of Erasmus's Colloquia familiaria (1518-1533), the dialogues that began as Latin conversation exercises and grew into some of the sharpest social commentary of the sixteenth century - a shipwreck at sea, a pilgrimage sent up as tourism, an abbot bested by a learned woman, Charon ferrying the war dead. Banned and bestselling at once, they were how generations of Europeans learned both spoken Latin and Erasmian irony.
